subtopic_detail: Long term lithium monitoring and hypercalcaemia
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 46 year old woman in the community clinic. She has bipolar I disorder and has taken lithium carbonate 750 mg nightly for 12 years with no relapse in that time. She feels well and adherent.

She mentions six months of constipation and vague aches. Her general practitioner has sent through a routine annual panel taken 12 hours post dose. She takes no diuretic, calcium supplement or vitamin D. Her thyroid function is within normal limits and she has had no recent immobilisation or fracture.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74, BP 126/78, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.68 mmol/L (0.6-0.8); corrected calcium 2.74 mmol/L (2.10-2.60); phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (0.75-1.50)
data_table.Blood tests: Creatinine 82 micromol/L (45-90); eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73m2; TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Measure serum parathyroid hormone alongside a repeat corrected calcium level
options.rationale: Lithium reduces the sensitivity of the parathyroid calcium sensing receptor and causes a parathyroid hormone dependent hypercalcaemia that is inappropriately non suppressed; a paired parathyroid hormone and calcium is the test that separates this from malignancy or vitamin D excess (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).

options.text: Reduce the lithium dose by 25 per cent and recheck the trough level in one week
options.rationale: The lithium level is mid range and the calcium abnormality is not dose dependent toxicity, so dose reduction neither explains nor corrects the hypercalcaemia and risks losing 12 years of mood stability (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Cease lithium today and substitute sodium valproate as maintenance monotherapy
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium cessation carries a rebound mania risk and the hypercalcaemia has not yet been characterised biochemically; any switch decision follows the parathyroid hormone result rather than preceding it (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Commence a thiazide diuretic to lower urinary calcium and repeat the panel monthly
options.rationale: Thiazides raise serum calcium and reduce renal lithium clearance, so this worsens both problems at once; thiazides are used for lithium induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, which is a different complication (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Arrange a bone mineral density scan and start weekly oral alendronate therapy
options.rationale: Antiresorptive therapy treats a consequence rather than establishing the cause, and starting it before the parathyroid hormone is known will confound later interpretation of bone turnover (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Lithium associated hyperparathyroidism affects up to 10 per cent of patients on long term therapy and is often missed because calcium is not always on the routine lithium panel. It differs from primary hyperparathyroidism in that the parathyroid glands are frequently diffusely hyperplastic rather than a single adenoma. The abnormality can persist after lithium cessation, so stopping the drug is not a reliable cure and is rarely the first move in a patient who has been well for over a decade. Management is shared between psychiatry and endocrinology and weighs relapse risk against the degree of hypercalcaemia.
key_points: Corrected calcium belongs on the annual lithium panel alongside creatinine, eGFR and thyroid function
Lithium hypercalcaemia is parathyroid hormone dependent, so parathyroid hormone will be normal or high rather than suppressed
Thiazides both raise calcium and reduce lithium clearance and are the wrong agent here
Hypercalcaemia may persist after lithium is stopped because of parathyroid hyperplasia
explanation.pearls: Lithium also causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and reduced eGFR, so an annual panel needs calcium, creatinine, eGFR and thyroid function together; a trough level alone will look reassuring while calcium climbs.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

subtopic_detail: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis thresholds at new HIV diagnosis
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 41 year old man in the ambulatory clinic two weeks after a new diagnosis of human immunodeficiency virus infection made on serology and confirmed by a second assay. He feels well, has gained no weight recently and has no cough, fever or oral lesions.

He has never taken antiretroviral therapy. He has no allergies, in particular no sulfonamide allergy, and his liver function is within normal limits. His chest radiograph is clear and his cryptococcal antigen is negative. His baseline results are now available and he is keen to begin treatment today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 124/78, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: CD4 count 140 cells/microlitre (500-1500); HIV viral load 82000 copies/mL; cryptococcal antigen negative; chest radiograph clear
data_table.Blood tests: Full blood count, electrolytes and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to commence today?

options.text: Antiretroviral therapy alone, with prophylaxis added only if the CD4 count falls further
options.rationale: The CD4 count is already below the 200 cells per microlitre threshold at which Pneumocystis prophylaxis is indicated, so waiting for a further fall leaves the highest risk period uncovered (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Antiretroviral therapy plus azithromycin weekly for disseminated mycobacterial prophylaxis
options.rationale: Azithromycin prophylaxis against Mycobacterium avium complex applies below 50 cells per microlitre, and this near pair threshold is the point of the distinction (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Antiretroviral therapy plus daily co-trimoxazole for Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis
options.rationale: Antiretroviral therapy is started at diagnosis regardless of CD4 count, and a CD4 below 200 cells per microlitre triggers co-trimoxazole prophylaxis until immune reconstitution is sustained (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Management Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Deferred antiretroviral therapy until the CD4 count recovers above 350 cells per microlitre
options.rationale: Deferring treatment reflects superseded practice; immediate therapy at diagnosis improves survival and reduces transmission irrespective of CD4 count (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Antiretroviral therapy plus fluconazole daily for prevention of cryptococcal meningitis
options.rationale: Primary antifungal prophylaxis is not routine in Australia and the cryptococcal antigen screen is negative, so this adds toxicity and interactions without benefit (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Management Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Antiretroviral therapy is now started at diagnosis in every person with human immunodeficiency virus infection regardless of CD4 count, which was a substantial change from earlier deferred strategies. Opportunistic infection prophylaxis is layered on top according to CD4 thresholds, and the two decisions are made independently at the same visit. The main thresholds worth memorising are 200 cells per microlitre for Pneumocystis and toxoplasmosis prophylaxis and 50 cells per microlitre for Mycobacterium avium complex. Prophylaxis is stopped once the CD4 count has been sustained above threshold on suppressive therapy, typically for at least three to six months.
key_points: Start antiretroviral therapy at diagnosis irrespective of CD4 count
CD4 below 200 cells per microlitre triggers co-trimoxazole prophylaxis
CD4 below 50 cells per microlitre triggers azithromycin for Mycobacterium avium complex
Cease prophylaxis once the CD4 count is sustained above threshold on suppressive therapy
explanation.pearls: Screen for cryptococcal antigen when the CD4 count is below 100 cells per microlitre before starting antiretroviral therapy; unmasking an occult cryptococcal infection as immune reconstitution syndrome carries a far higher mortality than treating it first.

subtopic_detail: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis after an earlier sensitising event
stem:
You are the registrar in the antenatal clinic seeing a 27 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 28 weeks. She is blood group O RhD negative and her partner's group is unknown.

At 20 weeks she had a small painless vaginal bleed, was assessed in the day unit and received a dose of anti-D immunoglobulin at that time with a Kleihauer showing no excess foetal cells. She has had no bleeding since and reports normal foetal movements. Her antibody screen taken today is negative and her foetal morphology scan at 20 weeks was reported as normal with a posterior placenta clear of the os. She asks whether she needs anything further before delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 112/68, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6, foetal heart rate 142
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O RhD negative; antibody screen negative today; symphysis fundal height appropriate for dates

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: No further anti-D immunoglobulin, since a dose was already given for the bleed at 20 weeks
options.rationale: Anti-D given for a sensitising event does not substitute for routine antenatal prophylaxis, because the protection from that dose has waned well before the third trimester (Source: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin).
source_refs: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

options.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin 250 international units now and repeat the same dose at 34 weeks gestation
options.rationale: The 250 international unit dose is the near pair used for first trimester sensitising events, whereas routine third trimester prophylaxis requires the larger dose (Source: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin).
source_refs: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

options.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin 625 international units now and repeat the same dose at 34 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Australian practice for a non sensitised RhD negative woman is routine antenatal prophylaxis with 625 international units at both 28 and 34 weeks, independent of any earlier event based dose (Source: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin; National Blood Authority).
source_refs: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

options.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin deferred until after delivery once the cord blood group has been determined
options.rationale: Postnatal prophylaxis is given in addition to antenatal doses, and deferring the antenatal doses leaves the third trimester unprotected against silent transplacental haemorrhage (Source: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin).
source_refs: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

options.text: Kleihauer testing today with anti-D immunoglobulin given only if foetal cells are demonstrated
options.rationale: Kleihauer testing quantifies bleeding after a sensitising event to determine whether extra doses are needed, and it is not a gate for routine antenatal prophylaxis (Source: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin).
source_refs: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis reduced the rate of RhD alloimmunisation from around 1 per cent to well under 0.5 per cent by covering silent transplacental haemorrhage that produces no symptoms. Australian practice gives 625 international units at 28 and 34 weeks to every non sensitised RhD negative woman, then a further 625 international units within 72 hours of birth if the baby is RhD positive. Event based doses for bleeding, amniocentesis, external cephalic version, abdominal trauma or termination are given in addition to and never instead of the routine schedule. Once anti-D antibodies are genuinely present from prior sensitisation, prophylaxis no longer has a role and management shifts to titre surveillance and middle cerebral artery Doppler.
key_points: Routine antenatal prophylaxis is 625 international units at 28 and 34 weeks in Australia
Event based doses are additional to, not a substitute for, the routine schedule
The first trimester sensitising event dose is 250 international units
A positive antibody screen from established sensitisation means prophylaxis no longer applies
explanation.pearls: A passively acquired anti-D from prophylaxis can appear on an antibody screen at a low titre for up to eight weeks; check the timing of the last dose before treating a weak positive screen as true sensitisation.

sources.label: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

subtopic_detail: Initial treatment of steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome in a preschool child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 4 year old boy whose parents noticed his eyes were puffy in the mornings for the past week, and that his tummy now looks swollen. He is otherwise well, eating and playing normally.

He has had no fever, rash or joint swelling, and his urine has been pale rather than dark or tea coloured. He was born at term with no antenatal renal abnormality and has no family history of kidney disease. On examination he has periorbital oedema, mild ascites and pitting oedema to mid shin. His blood pressure is on the 50th centile for age and height. His urine microscopy shows no red cell casts.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 92/58, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein creatinine ratio 640 mg/mmol; urine microscopy no red cell casts; complement C3 and C4 within normal limits
data_table.Blood tests: Serum albumin 17 g/L (35-50); creatinine 32 micromol/L (25-55); total cholesterol 9.2 mmol/L (below 4.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Percutaneous renal biopsy before any treatment to establish the underlying histological diagnosis
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for atypical features such as age under one or over twelve years, hypertension, haematuria with casts, low complement or renal impairment, none of which is present (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic Syndrome).

options.text: Oral prednisolone daily for four to six weeks followed by an alternate day tapering course
options.rationale: Typical childhood nephrotic syndrome between one and twelve years with normal blood pressure, normal complement and no active urinary sediment is treated empirically with corticosteroid without biopsy, since around 90 per cent are steroid sensitive minimal change disease (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic Syndrome).

options.text: Intravenous albumin infusion followed by intravenous furosemide to mobilise the accumulated oedema
options.rationale: Albumin with diuretic is reserved for symptomatic oedema such as respiratory compromise, scrotal or vulval oedema or skin breakdown, and it carries pulmonary oedema risk in a child who is well (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic Syndrome).

options.text: Oral furosemide with strict fluid restriction and daily weights until the oedema has resolved
options.rationale: Diuretics in an intravascularly depleted child risk hypovolaemia and thrombosis, and they do nothing to treat the underlying glomerular protein leak (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic Syndrome).

options.text: Oral enalapril to reduce proteinuria with monitoring of renal function and serum potassium
options.rationale: Angiotensin blockade is an adjunct in steroid resistant or persistently proteinuric disease rather than initial therapy in a previously untreated child (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic Syndrome).

explanation.summary: Childhood nephrotic syndrome is defined by heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, and in the one to twelve year age group it is overwhelmingly steroid sensitive minimal change disease. Treatment is therefore started empirically without histology, and biopsy is reserved for atypical features or steroid resistance after four weeks of daily therapy. The important early complications are hypovolaemia, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis from urinary loss of immunoglobulin and complement factors, and venous thrombosis from loss of antithrombin III. Families are taught home urine dipstick monitoring because relapse is common and early detection shortens the treatment course.
key_points: Age one to twelve with normal blood pressure and no active sediment means treat without biopsy
Around 90 per cent of this group are steroid sensitive
Albumin with diuretic is reserved for symptomatic oedema, not routine treatment
Watch for peritonitis and thrombosis as the major early complications
explanation.pearls: Any child with nephrotic syndrome and abdominal pain needs spontaneous bacterial peritonitis excluded, with pneumococcus the commonest organism; ascitic tap and intravenous cefotaxime should not wait for a fever, which is often absent on corticosteroids.

subtopic_detail: Delusional disorder versus schizophreniform and brief psychotic disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 34 year old accountant referred by his general practitioner. For five months he has been convinced that a neighbour is adding a chemical to his rainwater tank to make him unwell. He has photographed the neighbour's fence line and lodged two council complaints.

He has continued full time work throughout and his performance review last month was unremarkable. He describes no voices, his speech is linear and goal directed, and his self care and social contact are unchanged. There is no elevated or depressed mood, and a urine drug screen taken today is negative.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: euthymic, reactive affect, linear speech, no perceptual disturbance, insight absent regarding the belief
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; full blood count, electrolytes and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder with a persecutory theme following a psychosocial stressor
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder requires the disturbance to resolve within one month and return to premorbid function, whereas this belief has persisted continuously for five months (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia).

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder given the duration falls between one month and six months
options.rationale: Schizophreniform disorder is the near pair here but still requires two or more criterion A features such as hallucinations, disorganised speech or negative symptoms, and only an isolated delusion is present (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia).

options.text: Delusional disorder of the persecutory type with preserved psychosocial functioning
options.rationale: A single non bizarre delusion lasting at least one month, with no hallucinations, no disorganisation, no negative symptoms and function outside the delusional theme largely intact, defines delusional disorder (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia).

options.text: Paranoid personality disorder with an overvalued idea about a neighbour dispute
options.rationale: Personality disorder produces pervasive lifelong suspiciousness across many relationships rather than one encapsulated belief held with delusional conviction over five months (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Personality Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Personality Disorders

options.text: Substance induced psychotic disorder related to undisclosed stimulant or cannabis use
options.rationale: The negative urine drug screen and the five month continuous course without intoxication or withdrawal periods argue against a substance induced picture (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Delusional disorder is under recognised because sufferers present to police, councils and lawyers long before psychiatry, and their preserved function makes clinicians doubt a psychotic diagnosis. The core discriminators are duration of at least one month, absence of other criterion A symptoms, and function that is impaired only where the delusion intrudes. Treatment response to antipsychotics is more modest than in schizophrenia and engagement is the main challenge given absent insight. Untreated cases can escalate to litigation, stalking or assault of the perceived persecutor, so risk assessment matters as much as the label.
key_points: Delusional disorder needs one month minimum of delusions and no other prominent criterion A symptoms
Brief psychotic disorder resolves within one month; schizophreniform runs one to six months but needs two criterion A features
Function outside the delusional theme is characteristically preserved
Assess risk to the person named in the delusion at every review
explanation.pearls: Delusional disorder subtypes include persecutory, jealous, erotomanic, somatic and grandiose; the somatic subtype most often presents to dermatology or infectious diseases rather than to psychiatry.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Personality Disorders

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis treatment selection after a positive interferon gamma release assay
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the refugee health clinic. A 26 year old man who arrived from Nepal 11 months ago has been referred after a positive interferon gamma release assay performed during a pre employment health check for aged care work.

He is entirely asymptomatic with no cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss. Two sputum samples collected for completeness were negative on smear and on culture at six weeks. His chest radiograph reported today shows clear lung fields with no apical scarring, cavitation or hilar lymphadenopathy. He takes no medication, drinks no alcohol, and has normal liver function with a negative human immunodeficiency virus serology. He asks how long treatment will take because he is due to start work.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Investigations: Interferon gamma release assay positive; chest radiograph clear; sputum smear and culture negative; HIV serology negative
data_table.Blood tests: Liver function and full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for two months then continuation phase
options.rationale: Four drug therapy treats active disease, which has been excluded by symptoms, a clear chest radiograph and negative cultures, and it exposes him to unnecessary hepatotoxicity (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Guidelines).

options.text: No treatment at present, with a repeat interferon gamma release assay in twelve months
options.rationale: The assay does not distinguish latent from past infection and does not revert usefully, so repeating it adds nothing while leaving a treatable reactivation risk in an aged care worker (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Guidelines).

options.text: Bacille Calmette Guerin vaccination now with annual symptom review by the general practitioner
options.rationale: Vaccination has no role after infection has already occurred and does not reduce reactivation risk from established latent infection (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Rifampicin daily for four months with baseline and interval liver function monitoring
options.rationale: Four months of daily rifampicin is a recommended Australian latent tuberculosis regimen with completion rates and hepatotoxicity superior to nine months of isoniazid, which suits a young man with normal liver function starting work (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Pyrazinamide with rifampicin for two months and fortnightly liver function monitoring throughout
options.rationale: The two month rifampicin and pyrazinamide combination was abandoned because of severe hepatotoxicity and fatalities and is no longer recommended for latent infection (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection is diagnosed when an immunological test is positive and active disease has been excluded clinically, radiologically and where indicated microbiologically. Excluding active disease first is not a formality, because treating active tuberculosis with a single drug generates resistance. Australian regimen options are isoniazid for six to nine months, rifampicin for four months, or weekly rifapentine and isoniazid for three months, with the shorter rifamycin based regimens preferred for completion and hepatic safety. Rifampicin induces cytochrome P450 enzymes, so a medication review for interactions with oral contraceptives, anticoagulants and antiretrovirals is part of prescribing.
key_points: Exclude active disease before treating latent infection to avoid generating resistance
Four months of daily rifampicin is preferred over nine months of isoniazid for completion and hepatic safety
Interferon gamma release assays do not distinguish latent from treated past infection
Rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer and needs a full interaction check
explanation.pearls: Warn any patient starting rifampicin that it turns urine, tears and sweat orange and permanently stains soft contact lenses; unexplained discolouration is the commonest reason for self cessation in the first fortnight.

subtopic_detail: Bundle of care in threatened preterm birth before 30 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a level 4 regional hospital assessing a 31 year old woman in her second pregnancy at 29 weeks and 3 days. She has had regular painful contractions every four minutes for two hours.

Speculum examination shows a closed cervix visually but digital examination finds the cervix 3 cm dilated and 80 per cent effaced. Her membranes are intact. She has had no corticosteroids in this pregnancy. She is afebrile with no uterine tenderness and her urinalysis and high vaginal swab show no evidence of infection. The cardiotocograph is reassuring with a baseline of 145 and normal variability. The neonatal unit here manages babies from 32 weeks and the tertiary centre is 90 minutes away by road.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7, foetal heart rate baseline 145
data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm dilated, 80 per cent effaced, membranes intact, vertex presenting
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph reassuring with normal variability; urinalysis and high vaginal swab show no evidence of infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intramuscular betamethasone, intravenous magnesium sulfate and transfer to the tertiary centre
options.rationale: Below 30 weeks with birth anticipated within 24 hours the bundle is antenatal corticosteroid for lung maturity, magnesium sulfate for foetal neuroprotection, and in utero transfer to a unit that can care for the gestation (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline

options.text: Intramuscular betamethasone alone with observation in the birth suite and reassessment in six hours
options.rationale: Corticosteroid is essential but omitting magnesium sulfate forgoes a proven reduction in cerebral palsy at this gestation, and staying in a unit that cannot care for a 29 week neonate risks ex utero transfer (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate alone with transfer arranged once contractions have been suppressed
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate provides neuroprotection but does not mature the lungs, and antenatal corticosteroid is the single intervention with the largest mortality benefit at this gestation (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline

options.text: Oral nifedipine tocolysis alone with reassessment of the cervix after four hours of treatment
options.rationale: Tocolysis has a supporting role to buy time for corticosteroids and transfer but does not improve neonatal outcomes on its own, so it is never the whole plan (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin for group B streptococcus prophylaxis with observation in the birth suite
options.rationale: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated once preterm labour is established, but giving it in isolation omits the two interventions that change neonatal mortality and neurological outcome (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline

explanation.summary: Threatened preterm birth is managed as a bundle rather than a single decision, and the components are corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate where the gestation qualifies, consideration of tocolysis, intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis and in utero transfer. Antenatal corticosteroids are given between 24 and 34 weeks and reduce respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage and neonatal death. Magnesium sulfate for foetal neuroprotection is given below 30 weeks when birth is expected within 24 hours, with a number needed to treat of about 60 to prevent one case of cerebral palsy. Tocolysis is used to create the window for the other interventions rather than to prolong pregnancy for its own sake, and in utero transfer consistently outperforms transferring a sick neonate afterwards.
key_points: Antenatal corticosteroids apply from 24 to 34 weeks and carry the largest mortality benefit
Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection applies below 30 weeks with birth expected within 24 hours
Tocolysis buys time for steroids and transfer rather than improving neonatal outcome itself
In utero transfer produces better outcomes than transferring a preterm neonate after birth
explanation.pearls: Betamethasone gives its full benefit from 24 hours after the first dose and persists for about seven days; a birth occurring even a few hours after the first dose still confers measurable benefit, so never withhold it because delivery looks imminent.

sources.label: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline
Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth National Clinical Practice Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Renal surveillance schedule after Henoch Schonlein purpura
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6 year old girl in the short stay unit. Over four days she has developed a rash over her buttocks and the backs of her legs that her mother describes as raised purple spots that do not fade when pressed, along with sore swollen ankles and intermittent tummy pain.

She is afebrile and looks well between episodes of pain. Her platelet count and coagulation screen are within normal limits, which excludes a bleeding disorder as the cause of the rash. Her abdomen is soft with no mass, guarding or rectal bleeding. Her blood pressure is on the 60th centile for age and height and her creatinine is within normal limits. Her urinalysis today shows blood 2+ and protein 1+.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 98/60, RR 20, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura over buttocks and extensor surfaces of both legs; bilateral ankle swelling; abdomen soft, no mass
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis blood 2+ and protein 1+; urine protein creatinine ratio 42 mg/mmol; platelets, coagulation screen and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow up plan?

options.text: No specific renal follow up is required, since the rash and joint symptoms resolve spontaneously
options.rationale: Nephritis is the complication that determines long term outcome and can appear or progress weeks after the rash has faded, so discharge without surveillance misses it (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

options.text: Renal biopsy arranged within the next fortnight to grade the severity of the glomerular involvement
options.rationale: Biopsy is indicated for nephrotic range proteinuria, impaired renal function or persistent significant proteinuria rather than for mild haematuria and proteinuria at presentation (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

options.text: Oral prednisolone for four weeks to prevent progression of the renal involvement over time
options.rationale: Corticosteroids shorten abdominal and joint pain but have not been shown to prevent or alter the course of nephritis, which is the widespread misconception this option tests (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

options.text: Weekly blood pressure and urinalysis for the first month, then at decreasing intervals to twelve months
options.rationale: Australian practice is structured surveillance with blood pressure and urinalysis, most intensively in the first one to two months when nephritis usually declares itself, continuing to six or twelve months (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound now and repeated at six months to assess for structural renal damage
options.rationale: Ultrasound assesses structure and is used to exclude intussusception in the abdominal form, but it does not detect the glomerular disease that surveillance is designed to find (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

explanation.summary: Henoch Schonlein purpura is the commonest childhood vasculitis and the diagnosis is clinical, requiring palpable purpura with lower limb predominance plus at least one of arthritis or arthralgia, abdominal pain, or renal involvement. The rash, joints and gut symptoms are self limiting over days to weeks, but nephritis determines long term outcome and develops in around a third of children, usually within the first two months. Because nephritis can appear after the child has apparently recovered, the follow up schedule of blood pressure and urinalysis is the single most important part of management. Corticosteroids reduce the duration of abdominal and joint pain but do not prevent renal disease, which is why they are not given routinely.
key_points: Nephritis develops in about a third of children and usually within the first two months
Surveillance is blood pressure and urinalysis, most frequent early then tapering to twelve months
Corticosteroids help abdominal and joint pain but do not prevent nephritis
Intussusception is the important acute abdominal complication and is ileoileal rather than ileocolic
explanation.pearls: Intussusception complicating this vasculitis is typically ileoileal, so it is missed by the air enema that reduces the usual ileocolic form; ultrasound is the diagnostic test and surgical reduction is usually required.

subtopic_detail: Persistent psychosis after confirmed cannabis abstinence
stem:
You are the registrar in a youth mental health service seeing a 19 year old apprentice. Seven weeks ago he presented with persecutory beliefs and second person auditory hallucinations after two years of daily high potency cannabis use.

He stopped cannabis at that first presentation and has attended weekly, with supervised urine screens negative for cannabinoids on each of the last five visits. Despite this, he still hears two voices commenting through the day and believes his supervisor is recording him. He has withdrawn from his football team and his mother reports he now speaks little at home. He is sleeping and eating, and denies any plan to harm himself or others.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: guarded, restricted affect, ongoing auditory hallucinations, reduced spontaneous speech
data_table.Investigations: Five consecutive supervised urine drug screens negative; full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue abstinence monitoring alone and review again in a further four weeks
options.rationale: Symptoms attributable to cannabis alone would be expected to settle within about one month of abstinence, so continued watchful waiting delays treatment of an emerging primary disorder (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia).

options.text: Refer to the drug and alcohol service for relapse prevention as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Substance work remains important but cannot be the only intervention when psychosis has persisted seven weeks beyond verified abstinence and negative symptoms are emerging (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia).

options.text: Prescribe diazepam 5 mg twice daily for anxiety and arrange supportive counselling
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines treat neither hallucinations nor negative symptoms and carry dependence risk in a young person with a substance use history (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence a long acting injectable antipsychotic at the first treatment appointment
options.rationale: Depot formulation is the near pair to oral therapy but is reserved for established adherence problems or patient preference after an oral trial has established tolerability (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence oral risperidone with baseline metabolic screening and early psychosis referral
options.rationale: Psychosis persisting well beyond one month of verified abstinence, with emerging negative symptoms and functional decline, is treated as first episode psychosis with a low dose second generation antipsychotic and specialist early psychosis care (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: The distinction between a cannabis induced psychotic disorder and a first episode of a primary psychotic illness is made on the course after abstinence rather than at the index presentation. Symptoms that outlast roughly one month of verified abstinence, and the appearance of negative symptoms such as reduced speech and social withdrawal, point away from a purely substance induced picture. Duration of untreated psychosis is one of the few modifiable predictors of long term outcome, which is why deferring treatment has a real cost. Early psychosis services combine low dose antipsychotic therapy with vocational support, family work and ongoing substance intervention.
key_points: Verified abstinence, not self report, is what makes the substance induced versus primary distinction interpretable
Negative symptoms emerging during abstinence favour a primary psychotic disorder
Baseline weight, waist circumference, fasting glucose, lipids and prolactin precede antipsychotic initiation
Longer duration of untreated psychosis predicts poorer functional recovery
explanation.pearls: Start risperidone at 1 mg daily in first episode psychosis and titrate no faster than weekly; doses above 4 mg daily add extrapyramidal effects and prolactin elevation without improving response rates in this group.

subtopic_detail: Antiviral indication and agent choice in influenza with chronic airways disease
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68 year old woman during an influenza season. She describes 36 hours of fever, myalgia and a dry cough that began abruptly. A point of care nucleic acid test taken this morning is positive for influenza A.

She has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with a forced expiratory volume in one second of 52 per cent predicted and uses a long acting muscarinic antagonist and a long acting beta agonist daily. She has had two exacerbations in the last 12 months. She is not hypoxic, her chest is clear of focal crackles and her sputum has not changed colour or volume. Her creatinine and eGFR are within normal limits and she received the seasonal vaccine four weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 132/78, RR 20, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 38.2
data_table.Investigations: Influenza A nucleic acid test positive; chest auscultation clear with no focal crackles
data_table.Blood tests: Creatinine and eGFR within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Symptomatic treatment only, since antivirals are of benefit only within 24 hours of onset
options.rationale: The evidence based window for starting a neuraminidase inhibitor is 48 hours from symptom onset, and this presentation at 36 hours falls comfortably inside it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral oseltamivir twice daily for five days alongside her usual inhaled maintenance therapy
options.rationale: Antiviral therapy is recommended for confirmed influenza in patients at high risk of complications, which includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and age over 65, when started within 48 hours of onset (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Australian Influenza Guidelines).

options.text: Inhaled zanamivir twice daily for five days as the preferred agent in chronic airways disease
options.rationale: Inhaled zanamivir is the near pair but is specifically cautioned in asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease because it can precipitate bronchospasm (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for five days to cover secondary bacterial infection risk
options.rationale: There is no change in sputum volume or purulence and no focal findings, so empirical antibacterial therapy is not indicated at this point (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for five days as treatment for an infective exacerbation
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids are for an exacerbation defined by increased breathlessness, sputum volume or purulence, none of which is present, and they may prolong viral shedding (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

explanation.summary: Antiviral therapy for influenza is targeted rather than universal, and the decision rests on the presence of risk factors for complications rather than on symptom severity alone. Australian risk groups include people aged 65 and over, pregnant women, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, and those with chronic cardiac, respiratory, renal, neurological or metabolic disease or immunosuppression. Benefit is greatest when treatment starts within 48 hours of symptom onset, though therapy is still offered beyond that window to hospitalised or deteriorating patients. Vaccination reduces but does not eliminate risk, so a recent vaccine does not change the treatment decision once infection is confirmed.
key_points: Treat confirmed influenza in high risk groups within 48 hours of symptom onset
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and age over 65 are both independent risk criteria
Zanamivir is avoided in obstructive airways disease because of bronchospasm risk
Recent vaccination does not remove the indication for antiviral therapy
explanation.pearls: Oseltamivir needs renal dose adjustment once creatinine clearance falls below 60 mL/min, and this is the commonest prescribing error in the older patients who most need the drug.
